unit.title: Operate in a culturally diverse work environment

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is cultural diversity at work?
options: Everyone at work coming from the same background
A rule that all staff must speak in the same way
People of many backgrounds working together
A list of the countries that the guests come from

questions.stem: Which of these is part of a person's culture?
options: Their language, beliefs, customs and food
Their shoe size and how tall they are
The colour of the car that they drive
The number of their mobile phone

questions.stem: Jamaica's motto is "Out of Many, One People". What does it say about Jamaica?
options: All of its people first came from one single country
Only one group of people has ever lived on the island
Every visitor must become Jamaican to stay
Its people come from many roots but are one nation

questions.stem: How can a culturally diverse team help a villa?
options: It means nobody ever has to work together
It brings more ideas and languages
It means the rules are different for each worker
It stops the villa from welcoming any new guests

questions.stem: What is a stereotype?
options: A music system that is used to play songs at a party
A fixed idea that everyone in a group is the same
A fact that has been proved about one person
A friendly greeting used in many countries

questions.stem: Why are stereotypes harmful at work?
options: They help staff to serve every guest faster
They are only harmful when guests can hear them
They make staff learn much more about each guest
They lead to unfair treatment of people

questions.stem: What is prejudice?
options: Judging someone unfairly before you know them
Learning about a person's culture before you meet
Giving every guest the same high standard of care
Asking a guest politely what they would prefer

questions.stem: Which is an example of discrimination at work?
options: Giving a worker training in a new language
Giving a worker the day off that they asked for last week
Giving a worker fewer shifts because of their religion
Giving a worker praise for very good service

questions.stem: A guest arrives wearing a headscarf. What should you do?
options: Assume she will not want any dish on the menu
Ask her to take it off before she enters the villa
Welcome her like any guest and offer your help
Keep away from her in case you say the wrong thing

questions.stem: Why should you ask guests what they need, instead of guessing from where they come from?
options: People from one place can have very different needs
Guests prefer staff who never ask them any questions
Guessing is quicker, and guests do not really mind it
Where a guest comes from tells you all you need to know

questions.stem: Why should you take care with hand gestures when serving guests from other countries?
options: Guests from abroad cannot see hand gestures very well
Hand gestures are against the rules in tourism
Gestures mean exactly the same thing everywhere
A gesture that is polite here may be rude elsewhere

questions.stem: Some guests like you to stand further away from them than others do. What should you do?
options: Stand very close, to show that you are friendly
Notice their comfort and give them room
Touch their arm to help them relax and feel at home
Ignore it, since distance does not matter to anyone

questions.stem: A guest makes little eye contact when you speak. What is the best way to understand this?
options: In some cultures, less eye contact shows respect
The guest must be hiding something from you
The guest is being rude and should be told so
The guest does not want any service from you

questions.stem: You are not sure how to say a guest's name. What should you do?
options: Give them a nickname that is easier for you to say
Avoid using their name at all during their stay
Ask politely how to say it, then use it correctly
Make a joke about how hard the name is to say

questions.stem: Which of these should staff never joke about at work?
options: The sunny weather that day
A tasty dessert at lunch
A funny film they once saw
A person's race or religion

questions.stem: A guest who speaks little English wants to know the breakfast time. What is most helpful?
options: Say the time again, louder and faster
Show the time on a clock or write it down
Tell the guest to ask another guest
Say it once and then walk away

questions.stem: Which words are best when speaking to someone whose first language is not English?
options: Long words and plenty of local slang
Fast speech with lots of jokes
Short, simple words and sentences
Technical words from the trade

questions.stem: A colleague speaks the same language as a guest. How can they help?
options: They can help explain, so the guest is understood
They should take over all of your work for the day
They should laugh at the guest's mistakes in English
They should keep it secret that they speak it

questions.stem: How can you check that a guest who speaks little English has understood you?
options: Ask "Do you understand?" and accept a nod
Speak louder until the guest says "yes"
Assume they understood if they smile at you
Ask them to show you or repeat the key point

questions.stem: A guest tells you they eat only halal food. What should you do?
options: Serve pork, as long as it has been well cooked
Tell the cook, and check the ingredients used
Tell the guest that the villa cannot cater for it
Guess which of the dishes might be all right

questions.stem: What does a vegan diet leave out?
options: All animal foods, including eggs and milk
Only red meat, such as beef and pork
Only fish and other seafood
Only fruit and green vegetables

questions.stem: A guest is fasting during the day for religious reasons. How can you help?
options: Keep offering them lunch, to be friendly
Tell them that fasting is bad for them on holiday
Ask about suitable meal times and plan for them
Eat your lunch in front of them to tempt them

questions.stem: A guest asks for a quiet place to pray. What should you do?
options: Tell them that prayer is not allowed at the villa
Laugh, and remind them that they are on holiday
Send them to the busy kitchen, where there is space
Help them find a clean, quiet and private space

questions.stem: A guest follows a custom you have never seen before. What is the best response?
options: Tell them it is strange and that it should not be done
Show respect, and ask politely if you need to know
Ignore the custom and do things your own way
Call other staff over to come and watch it

questions.stem: Why should you learn about the customs of guests you often serve?
options: To serve them in a way that feels respectful
To make fun of their customs with colleagues
To tell them that their customs are wrong
To find reasons to avoid serving them

questions.stem: A new colleague, Ravi, has come to Jamaica from another country. How can you help him settle in?
options: Leave him alone until he has learned local ways
Only ever talk to him about his own country
Tell him to change his name so that he fits in better
Welcome him, explain how things work, include him

questions.stem: A colleague's accent is different from yours. What is respectful?
options: Copy the accent to make the others laugh
Ask them not to speak at all while at work
Listen carefully, and ask again if needed
Only ever speak to them by writing notes

questions.stem: Two colleagues from different backgrounds misunderstand each other. What is the best way to sort it out?
options: Tell them to keep away from each other from now on
Talk calmly and explain what each meant
Blame the one who is newest to the villa team
Ask the guests to decide which of them is right

questions.stem: You hear a colleague making racist remarks about a guest. What should you do?
options: Report it to your supervisor, as the policy says
Laugh, so the colleague does not feel awkward
Repeat the remarks to other staff for a joke
Tell the guest exactly what was said about them

questions.stem: A guest makes an offensive remark about a worker's religion. What should the worker do?
options: Make an offensive remark back about the guest
Refuse to serve any guests at all from now on
Post about the guest on social media that night
Stay calm, do not argue, and report it

questions.stem: What is unconscious bias?
options: A clear rule written in the staff handbook
A choice that is always fair and based on facts
A hidden preference we hold without knowing it
A kind of training that teaches a new language

questions.stem: Which is a good way to reduce your own bias at work?
options: Work only with people who are just like you
Check your first ideas against the facts
Trust your first idea about every guest you meet
Avoid learning anything about other cultures

questions.stem: A blind guest arrives with a trained dog that helps them get around. What should you do?
options: Ask the guest to leave the dog outside the villa gate
Pet and feed the dog to make it feel at home
Speak only to the guest's companion from now on
Welcome both, and do not distract the working dog

questions.stem: A guest who is deaf uses sign language. How can you communicate?
options: Face them, write notes and use simple gestures
Shout, so that they can hear you better
Talk to them with your back turned to them
Avoid speaking to them at all during their stay

questions.stem: An older guest takes longer to walk to the dining room. What is respectful?
options: Hurry them along so that dinner is not late
Walk at their pace and offer help if they wish
Tell them to stay in their room for meals
Walk on ahead and leave them to follow

questions.stem: A guest asks to be served only by staff of a certain race. What should staff do?
options: Agree at once and change the staff roster
Argue loudly with the guest in front of others
Pass it politely to the manager to deal with
Walk out and refuse to work at the villa again

questions.stem: Which is fair treatment of guests from different backgrounds?
options: The same high standard for every guest
Better service for guests from richer countries
Less service for guests who speak little English
Extra service only for guests who are like you

questions.stem: Why do workplaces have anti-discrimination policies?
options: To let the managers hire only their own friends and family
To stop staff from speaking other languages
To keep visitors from other countries away
So that everyone is treated fairly and with respect

questions.stem: Where can you find your villa's rules on respect and discrimination?
options: On the guest's booking form
In the staff handbook or code of conduct
In the cook's recipe book
On a tourist map of the parish

questions.stem: Which is a good way to learn about other cultures?
options: Rely on jokes and films about other countries
Assume all cultures are the same as your own
Ask respectful questions and listen to people
Keep away from people who are different

questions.stem: Guests are celebrating a holiday from their own country at the villa. What can staff do?
options: Ask how they celebrate it and help where suitable
Tell them that only Jamaican holidays are marked here
Ignore it, since it is not a Jamaican holiday
Ask them to keep the noise down all day long

questions.stem: A colleague wears religious dress that is different from yours. What is respectful?
options: Ask them to change it so they look like everyone else
Make comments about it to the other staff
Point it out to the guests so they can look
Accept it, as long as it meets safety rules

questions.stem: A guest says they do not eat beef for religious reasons. What should you do?
options: Serve beef anyway, but cut it up very small
Tell the guest the menu cannot be changed
Note it, tell the cook, and offer other dishes
Remove the beef from the plate just before serving

questions.stem: Why is it useful to think about your own culture and habits?
options: It proves that your way is always the right one
It shows you that your way is not the only way
It means you never need to change anything
It shows which guests deserve better service

questions.stem: A guest seems upset by something you said, but you are not sure why. What should you do?
options: Apologise and ask politely if you caused offence
Ignore it, since you did nothing wrong at all
Repeat it more loudly so that they understand
Tell them that they are being far too sensitive

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the word for the beliefs, customs, language and way of life shared by a group of people?
What word means treating someone unfairly because of their race, religion, age, sex or disability?
What word describes food prepared to meet Jewish dietary laws?
What is the name for communication without words, such as gestures, eye contact and facial expressions?
What do you call a person whose job is to turn spoken words from one language into another?
What do you call a person who eats no meat or fish, but may eat eggs and milk?
What word means accepting and respecting beliefs or customs that are different from your own?
What is the two-word name for the principle that every person gets the same fair chance at work, whatever their background?
What kind of trained dog helps a person who is blind to move around safely?
Which language, other than English, is spoken by many visitors from Latin America and Spain?
What two-word term names the area around a person's body that they feel is their own?
Which Jamaican dish, from the cooking of Indian Jamaicans, is made with goat meat and curry spices?
What is the name of the faith that began in Jamaica, honours Haile Selassie I, and whose followers often keep an ital diet?
What one word names a special day or time that a religion or culture celebrates every year, such as Diwali or Christmas?
What two-word term means being aware of other cultures and avoiding words or actions that may offend?

essays.stem: Explain what cultural diversity means in a villa workplace, and describe three benefits it brings.
essays.modelAnswer: Cultural diversity means that people from many different backgrounds work together and serve guests together. They may differ in culture, language, religion, race, age, gender, ability and life experience. At a villa, the guests may come from North America, Europe, Latin America, Asia or other Caribbean islands, and the staff may also come from different parishes, faiths and families. One benefit is better service: staff who understand different customs, or who speak another language, can make guests from many places feel at home. A second benefit is more ideas: people with different experiences solve problems in different ways and suggest new ways to please guests. A third benefit is a fairer, happier workplace: when everyone is respected, staff work better together, stay longer and feel proud of their work. Diversity also gives the villa a good name, because guests notice when they are treated with respect.
markingPoints: Explains cultural diversity: people of many backgrounds working together
Gives examples of ways people differ (language, religion, age, ability and so on)
Benefit: better service and guests from many places feel at home
Benefit: more ideas and better problem-solving
Benefit: a fairer, happier team and a better name for the villa

essays.stem: Explain what stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination are, and why each is harmful at work. Use workplace examples.
essays.modelAnswer: A stereotype is a fixed, over-simple idea that all people in a group are the same, for example believing that all young guests are noisy, or that all older guests dislike modern music. It is harmful because it stops us from seeing each person as an individual, and it can lead to poor service. Prejudice is judging someone, often unfairly, before you know them, usually because of a stereotype. For example, a worker may decide that a guest with a strong accent will be difficult before the guest has even asked for anything. It harms trust and makes people feel unwelcome. Discrimination is acting unfairly towards someone because of their race, religion, sex, age, disability or background, for example giving a colleague fewer shifts because of their faith, or giving a guest slower service. It is the most harmful, because it causes real loss and hurt, breaks the villa's rules, and can be against the law. All three damage teamwork and the villa's good name.
markingPoints: Stereotype explained, with a suitable example
Explains why stereotypes harm (people not seen as individuals, poor service)
Prejudice explained, with an example and its harm
Discrimination explained, with a workplace example
Explains that discrimination causes real harm, breaks rules and may be against the law

essays.stem: Describe how you would communicate with a guest who speaks very little English, to make sure their needs are met.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stay friendly and patient, smile and greet the guest, and show by my body language that I want to help. I would speak slowly and clearly, using short, simple words and sentences, and avoid slang, local words and jokes, which are hard to understand. I would not shout, because speaking louder does not help understanding. I would use other ways to communicate: pointing, simple gestures, pictures, menus with photos, maps, and writing down numbers such as times and prices. A translation app on the phone can help with key words. If a colleague speaks the guest's language, I would ask them to help. To check that the guest has understood, I would ask them to show me or repeat the main point, rather than just accepting a nod. I would write important information down for them, and tell my colleagues about the guest's needs so the whole team can help.
markingPoints: Stays friendly and patient
Speaks slowly with simple words; no slang or shouting
Uses gestures, pictures, written notes or a translation app
Asks a colleague who speaks the language to help
Checks understanding by asking the guest to show or repeat, and tells the team

essays.stem: Explain how body language and other non-verbal signals can differ between cultures, and how a villa worker can avoid giving offence.
essays.modelAnswer: Non-verbal communication is the message we send without words: gestures, facial expressions, eye contact, personal space, touch and tone of voice. These can mean different things in different cultures. A hand sign that is friendly in Jamaica may be rude somewhere else. In some cultures, looking someone straight in the eye shows honesty; in others, less eye contact shows respect, especially to older people. Some people are comfortable standing close and touching an arm; others prefer more space and no touch. To avoid giving offence, a villa worker should use simple, open body language: a warm smile, a polite nod, and an open hand to point instead of one finger. They should keep a comfortable distance and avoid touching guests unless it is needed, such as helping someone down a step, and ask first. They should watch how the guest behaves and follow their lead, learn about the customs of guests they often serve, and apologise politely if they get it wrong.
markingPoints: Explains what non-verbal communication is
Gestures can mean different things in different cultures
Eye contact, personal space and touch differ between cultures
Uses simple, open body language; keeps a comfortable distance and asks before touching
Follows the guest's lead, learns about customs, and apologises if wrong

essays.stem: Describe how a villa team can meet guests' religious and dietary needs without making assumptions.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should ask every guest about their needs, rather than guessing from their name, dress or country. This can be done politely on the booking form and again on arrival, for example: "Do you have any dietary needs, or anything we can do to make your stay comfortable?" The answers are written down and shared with the cook, the butler and the housekeepers. For food, the cook checks the ingredients and suppliers for needs such as halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan, no pork, no beef or no alcohol, and keeps those foods apart and clearly labelled. If a guest is fasting, the team asks about meal times and plans for them. For religious practice, staff can offer a clean, quiet space for prayer, give information about local places of worship, and respect days of rest and holidays. Staff should never make comments or jokes about a guest's beliefs. If the team is unsure, they ask the guest again, respectfully.
markingPoints: Asks every guest (booking and arrival) instead of guessing from name, dress or country
Records the needs and shares them with the whole team
Cook checks ingredients and keeps special foods apart and labelled
Plans for fasting, offers a prayer space, and respects days of rest
Never jokes about beliefs, and asks again respectfully when unsure

essays.stem: Describe how you would help a new colleague from a different country or background settle into the villa team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would welcome the new colleague warmly, introduce myself, and learn to say their name correctly. I would introduce them to the rest of the team and show them around the villa: where things are kept, the staff areas, the safety exits and the first-aid kit. I would explain how the villa works, including the rosters, the log book, the house rules and the standards for guests, using clear, simple words and checking that they understand. I would include them in breaks, conversations and team activities, so they do not feel left out. I would be patient while they learn local ways and words, and show interest in their culture, food and language, without making fun or asking rude questions. If they have needs, such as a time to pray or a special diet, I would help them speak to the supervisor. I would offer to answer questions at any time, and check how they are doing after the first week.
markingPoints: Welcomes them warmly and learns to say their name correctly
Introduces the team and shows them around, including safety points
Explains how the villa works and checks understanding
Includes them, is patient, and shows respectful interest in their culture
Helps with any needs through the supervisor and follows up

essays.stem: A guest is offended by something a worker said. Describe how the worker should deal with the situation.
essays.modelAnswer: The worker should notice the guest's reaction and take it seriously, even if they did not mean any harm. They should stay calm and not argue or defend themselves straight away. They should apologise sincerely, for example: "I am sorry if what I said upset you. That was not my intention." Then they should listen carefully and, if it is suitable, politely ask what caused offence, so they understand and do not repeat it. They should thank the guest for explaining. If the guest is still upset, the worker should tell their supervisor, who may also speak to the guest. Afterwards, the worker should think about what happened, learn more about the guest's culture or the meaning of the words used, and change how they speak. The worker should also tell the supervisor or write a short note in the log, so that the whole team can learn and avoid the same mistake with other guests.
markingPoints: Takes the reaction seriously and stays calm
Apologises sincerely
Listens, and politely asks what caused offence; thanks the guest
Involves the supervisor if the guest is still upset
Reflects, learns and records it so the team can learn

essays.stem: Explain what you would do if you saw a colleague treating a guest unfairly because of their background.
essays.modelAnswer: Treating a guest unfairly because of their race, religion, nationality, accent or other background is discrimination. It hurts the guest, breaks the villa's rules and code of conduct, may be against the law, and damages the villa's good name. If I saw it, I would first make sure the guest gets proper service, for example by stepping in politely to help them myself, without making a scene in front of other guests. I would not join in, laugh, or ignore it. If it is safe and suitable, I would speak to my colleague privately afterwards and explain calmly that their behaviour was unfair. I would then report what I saw to my supervisor, giving the facts: what happened, when and where, and who was there, as the villa's policy says. I would keep the matter confidential and not gossip about it. The supervisor can then deal with it and help the colleague learn, and the villa may want to apologise to the guest.
markingPoints: Recognises it as discrimination and explains the harm
Makes sure the guest is served properly, without a scene
Does not join in, laugh or ignore it
May speak calmly and privately to the colleague
Reports the facts to the supervisor as the policy says, and keeps it confidential

essays.stem: Explain how Jamaica's own mixed heritage, shown in the motto "Out of Many, One People", can help workers welcome visitors from many cultures.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica's people have roots in many places. Most Jamaicans are of African descent, and there are also people with Indian, Chinese, European and Middle Eastern roots, and many people of mixed heritage. Over time, these groups have shaped Jamaican food, music, faith and language: curry goat and roti came with Indian Jamaicans, and other dishes, words and customs came from other groups, mixing with African and European ways. The motto "Out of Many, One People" reminds us that people can be different and still live and work together as one. Jamaican workers can use this to welcome visitors. They already know, from their own lives, that differences in culture are normal and can be enjoyed. They can share the story of Jamaica's mixed heritage with guests, show curiosity and respect for the guests' own cultures, and treat every visitor with the same warmth. This helps visitors from any background feel at home.
markingPoints: Names several roots of Jamaica's people
Shows how these have shaped food, music, faith or language
Explains the meaning of the motto
Workers know from their own lives that cultural differences are normal
Workers share Jamaica's heritage, respect guests' cultures and give everyone the same warmth

essays.stem: Explain how a worker can become more culturally aware and reduce their own bias.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the worker can think about their own culture and habits, and accept that their way of doing things is not the only way. They can notice their first ideas about people, for example about a guest's dress or accent, and ask: "Is this based on facts, or on a stereotype?" They can learn about other cultures by asking respectful questions, listening to guests' and colleagues' stories, reading, and taking training on diversity and customer service. They can learn a few words of other languages, such as greetings in Spanish or French. They should get to know people who are different from them, at work and in the community. When they make a mistake, they should apologise, learn from it and change. They should also ask their supervisor and colleagues for feedback on how they treat others. Over time, this helps the worker treat every guest and colleague as an individual, fairly and with respect.
markingPoints: Reflects on own culture and accepts it is not the only way
Notices first ideas about people and checks them against facts
Learns about other cultures (questions, listening, reading, training, languages)
Gets to know people who are different from them
Learns from mistakes and feedback, treating each person as an individual

practical1.title: Make a 'Welcome in many languages' guest kit with a guest needs form
practical1.brief: Your group makes a welcome kit that a villa can use with guests who speak little English. It has three parts: (1) a poster or set of cards with 'hello', 'welcome', 'please', 'thank you', 'breakfast', 'toilet' and 'doctor' in English and at least four other languages that villa guests may speak (for example Spanish, French, German and Portuguese), with a simple guide to saying each; (2) picture cards for common guest needs (towels, water, taxi, meal times, pool rules); and (3) a one-page guest needs form that asks politely about language, diet, religious practice and access needs, without making assumptions. Each member makes at least one part and checks it with a reliable source (a dictionary, a teacher, or a translation app the Centre allows). Then the group uses the kit in a short role play with a 'guest' who speaks little English (the assessor or a trainee). Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the kit and a filled-in form.
materials: Card, poster paper, markers, coloured pencils, glue and scissors
A dictionary or phrase book, or a translation app the Centre allows
Sample pictures or simple icons for guest needs
Plain paper for the guest needs form
A phone or tablet for photos
photos: The group's plan, showing each member's part
A member checking a word or phrase with a reliable source
The finished language poster or cards
The picture cards for guest needs
The guest needs form, blank and then filled in
The role play, using the kit with the 'guest'
checklist: Made at least one part of the kit neatly and correctly
Checked words and phrases with a reliable source
Wrote the guest needs form in polite, respectful words, with no assumptions
Used simple words, gestures and the picture cards in the role play
Checked the guest's understanding by asking them to show or repeat
Showed respect and patience throughout, and helped others in the group
safety: Use scissors carefully and keep them closed when not in use
Use only websites and apps the Centre allows
Use made-up guest names on the form

practical2.title: Role-play serving guests with different cultural needs, and handle a misunderstanding
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group five situation cards, for example: a guest who eats only halal food; a guest who asks for a quiet place to pray; a guest who speaks little English and wants a taxi; a guest offended by a hand gesture; a colleague making a stereotyped remark about a guest. For each card, one member plays the villa worker, others play the guest or the colleague, and one member notes what was said. The worker must ask instead of assuming, show respect, and solve the situation politely. After each role play, the worker fills in either the guest needs form or a short incident note, and the group says one thing that went well and one thing to improve. Swap roles so that every member plays the worker at least once. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the forms and notes.
materials: Five situation cards from the assessor
Guest needs forms and incident note sheets
A simple villa set-up: a table, chairs, a phone and a menu
Pens, a clipboard, and a phone or tablet for photos
photos: The group's plan of who plays each part
The misunderstanding or stereotype role play
The completed forms and incident notes
checklist: Asked the guest about their needs instead of making assumptions
Used respectful words and body language, with no jokes about culture or religion
Spoke simply and checked understanding with the guest who speaks little English
Apologised and put things right when a guest was offended
Challenged or reported the stereotyped remark in the right way
Filled in the form or incident note clearly and accurately
safety: Role plays use words only: no pushing or touching
Use made-up names, and never mock any real culture, religion or person
Any member may stop a role play if they feel uncomfortable
Keep the area clear of trip hazards
